title: Rehras with others
hookLine: a household that prays Rehras together hears the day end the same way

lines: A PHONE PROPPED ON THE FRUIT BOWL.
cards: Seven-thirty in the evening, a small house in Birmingham. A father props his phone against the fruit bowl. On the screen: his sister in Toronto, still in afternoon light, her two kids squeezed into the frame.
He starts: so dar keha. His sister joins on the second line. The kids murmur, then catch up by the Chaupai.
Two cities, two clocks, one Rehras.

teach.h: ALONE, OR TOGETHER: HOME, GURDWARA, SCREEN.
teach.b: Rehras can be said alone, on a train, under your breath. It's also said together: a household in the front room, a congregation in the gurdwara in the evening, cousins on a video call across continents.
Why does that matter? Gurbani puts a lot of weight on sangat, the company of people who remember the One.

teach.h: SANGAT: WHERE THE ONE NAME IS SPOKEN.
teach.b: In Sri Raag, Guru Nanak asks how the true congregation is to be recognized, and answers, in paraphrase: it's where the One Name is spoken. Not where the building is grandest. Where the Name is.

teach.h: REHRAS KEEPS POINTING AT OTHER PEOPLE.
teach.b: Rehras keeps pointing at other people. Guru Nanak, stuck in the mud, sought the shelter of those who remember. Guru Arjan said join the company of the holy, and that whoever meets the true congregation is carried across.
There's something simpler, too. When a household says Rehras together, the children hear it before they can read it.
They learn where the pauses fall, which lines the grandmother says slowly, when everyone stands for Ardas.

teach.h: A HOUSE WITH A SHARED CLOCK.
teach.b: A day that ends the same way for everyone gives the house a shared clock. Even after an argument at dinner, everyone hears the same words: joy has come, mother; protect me with your hand; may all be well.
Saying it together doesn't erase the argument. But it's hard to stay quite as far apart after you've stood side by side for Ardas.

how: Rehras Sahib is recited in the evening in gurdwaras with the sangat, and families often say it together at home, one person often leading, ending with Ardas said standing; some families now join by phone or video across cities.

o: a family prayer said privately, on your own
the company of people who remember the One

games.q: you live alone, far from family, and want to say Rehras with others. what's open to you?
o: nothing: only a household together counts.
the gurdwara's evening sangat, or praying with someone by phone.
only a priest can lead it for you.
games.why: gurdwaras hold Rehras in the evening, and some families now pray it together by phone; sangat is where the Name is spoken.

practice: Think of someone you could end a day with: a partner, a child, a parent, a friend far away.
Picture the two of you sharing a small piece of it, two lines of the Chaupai, one quiet minute, a shared thank you, side by side or by phone. If you pray, say Waheguru once, for them.

wordCard.voice: Sangat, the congregation: the evening prayer said together, at home, in the gurdwara or across a screen, so a household and a sangat hear the day end the same way.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: sangat, the congregation, the company of those who remember the One.

carryVoice: Your line: end the day together. A shared minute is a beginning. I'm glad you came.
